---
title: "Data, Variables and Methods"
---

## Data

The data come from the EDUMERCO dataset, a survey conducted as part of the EDUMER-funded project that focused on beliefs and attitudes toward meritocracy and inequality. The survey was conducted in 2025 via Computer-Assisted Web Interviewing (CAWI) among adults aged 18 to 75 in the Santiago Metropolitan Region of Chile. The sampling design was a quota-based non-probability sample, with quotas for age, sex, educational level, and socioeconomic status that approximated the population parameters. The total sample consisted of 3,470 respondents, while the analytical sample consisted of 2,489 respondents.

## Variables

The dependent variable of this study is the preference for market justice in education. This construct is measured using the following statement: “It is just that high-income people have a better education for their children than people with lower incomes” (“Es justo que las personas de altos ingresos tengan una mejor educación para sus hijos que las personas con ingresos más bajos” in Spanish). The response categories are on a four-point Likert scale from (1) “strongly disagree” to (4) “strongly agree”. 

The main independent variable in this study is meritocratic beliefs. To this end, two areas are distinguished: (1) meritocratic perceptions and preferences, and (2) perceptions and acceptance of privilege. Meritocratic and privilege-based perceptions and preferences were measured using the same items proposed in the original scale [@castillo_multidimensional_2023]. The dimensions are summarized in @tbl-beliefs.

| Dimension | Type | Description |
|:----------|:-----|:------------|
| Meritocratic perceptions | Perception | Extent to which effort and ability are rewarded in Chile |
| Meritocratic preferences | Preference | Agreement that those who work harder or are more talented should be better rewarded |
| Privilege perceptions | Perception | Extent to which success is perceived as linked to connections and family wealth |
| Privilege acceptance | Preference | Agreement that it is acceptable for individuals with better connections or wealthy parents to achieve greater success |

: Dimensions of meritocratic beliefs {#tbl-beliefs}

Each item is rated on a four-point Likert scale ranging from “strongly disagree” (1) to “strongly agree” (4), higher
scores indicate stronger endorsement of the corresponding perception or preference.

In addition, other independent variables considered are educational level, income and political identification. Educational level is measured using the question: “What is the most recent course or level of study you completed?”. The response categories range from 1 to 9, where higher values indicate a higher level of education among respondents. This variable was subsequently dichotomized to examine differences between individuals with and without higher education. Income was measured using a question asking about the person's monthly income, with 10 response categories. For modeling purposes, this variable was recategorized into 5 categories, expressed as quintiles. Finally, political identification is measured along a left-right axis using a 6-category scale, where 1 indicates right, 5 indicates left, and 6 indicates independent. This variable was recategorized, resulting in four categories: left, center, right, and does not identify

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false

if (!require("pacman")) install.packages("pacman")

pacman::p_load(tidyverse,
               here,
               sjlabelled,
               knitr,
               kableExtra)

options(scipen=999)
rm(list = ls())

# 2. Data -----------------------------------------------------------------

here::i_am("paper/03-metodologia.qmd")
load(here::here("paper", "input/data/proc/db_proc.RData"))

# 3. Variables ------------------------------------------------------------

# db_proc.RData is already processed (see procesamiento/proc-data.r).
# Recodings below are the same ones used in the models of the results chapter
# (04-resultados-esp.qmd).

vars_m <- c("perc_effort", "perc_talent", "perc_rich_parents", "perc_contact",
            "pref_effort", "pref_talent", "pref_rich_parents", "pref_contact")

# income quintiles (approximate, since income is collected in 10 ordered brackets)
income_levels <- c(
  "Menos de $280.000 mensuales liquidos",
  "De $280.001 a $380.000 mensuales liquidos",
  "De $380.001 a $470.000 mensuales liquidos",
  "De $470.001 a $610.000 mensuales liquidos",
  "De $610.001 a $730.000 mensuales liquidos",
  "De $730.001 a $890.000 mensuales liquidos",
  "De $890.001 a $1.100.000 mensuales liquidos",
  "De $1.100.001 a $2.700.000 mensuales liquidos",
  "De $2.700.001 a $4.100.000 mensuales liquidos",
  "Mas de $4.100.001 mensuales liquidos"
)
income_code   <- as.integer(factor(db$income, levels = income_levels))
income_breaks <- unique(quantile(income_code, seq(0, 1, .2), type = 1, na.rm = TRUE))

db_desc <- db %>%
  mutate(
    sex      = factor(if_else(sex == 1, "Male", "Female"), levels = c("Male", "Female")),
    # educ is coded 1-9; 7-9 = university or more
    educ     = factor(if_else(educ >= 7, "University education", "No university education"),
                      levels = c("No university education", "University education")),
    income_5 = cut(income_code, breaks = income_breaks, include.lowest = TRUE,
                   labels = paste0("Q", seq_len(length(income_breaks) - 1))),
    pol      = factor(pol, levels = c("Left", "Center", "Right", "Does not identify"))
  )

var_labels <- c(
  just_educ         = "Education market justice preferences",
  perc_effort       = "Effort perception",
  perc_talent       = "Talent perception",
  perc_rich_parents = "Rich parents perception",
  perc_contact      = "Contact perception",
  pref_effort       = "Effort preference",
  pref_talent       = "Talent preference",
  pref_rich_parents = "Rich parents preference",
  pref_contact      = "Contact preference",
  sex               = "Sex",
  educ              = "University education",
  income_5          = "Income quintile",
  pol               = "Political identification"
)

# variables grouped as they appear in the table (Likert items keep their 1-4 scale)
var_groups <- list(
  "Dependent variable"         = "just_educ",
  "Meritocratic beliefs" = vars_m,
  "Covariates"                 = c("sex", "educ", "income_5", "pol")
)

# frequency table of a variable, categories in their natural order
freq_tab <- function(v) {
  x <- as.factor(db_desc[[v]])
  tibble(variable = var_labels[[v]],
         category = sub("esagree", "isagree", levels(x)),
         n        = as.integer(table(x)),
         pct      = n / sum(n) * 100)
}

desc_tbl <- imap_dfr(var_groups, function(vs, g) {
  map_dfr(vs, freq_tab) %>% mutate(group = g)
}) %>%
  mutate(group = factor(group, levels = names(var_groups))) %>%
  dplyr::select(group, variable, category, n, pct)

group_index <- desc_tbl %>% count(group) %>% tibble::deframe()

out_format <- if (knitr::is_latex_output()) "latex" else "html"

tab_desc <- desc_tbl %>%
  dplyr::select(-group) %>%
  mutate(pct = sprintf("%.1f", pct)) %>%
  rename(Variable = variable, Category = category, `Valid N` = n, `%` = pct) %>%
  kbl(format = out_format,
      align = "llrr",
      booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed", "responsive"),
                latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"),
                full_width = FALSE,
                font_size = 13) %>%
  collapse_rows(columns = 1, valign = "top") %>%
  pack_rows(index = group_index)

# save the table so it can be reused in other .qmd documents:
#   tab_desc <- readRDS(here::here("paper", "output", "tbl-desc.rds")); tab_desc
#   (tbl-desc-data.rds holds the underlying data frame)
saveRDS(tab_desc, here::here("paper", "output", "tbl-desc.rds"))
saveRDS(desc_tbl, here::here("paper", "output", "tbl-desc-data.rds"))

```

## Analytical strategy

The analysis proceeds in three steps. First, a latent profile analysis (LPA) identifies subgroups of respondents that share a common configuration of meritocratic perceptions and preferences. Second, each respondent is assigned to the profile to which they most likely belong. Third, an ordinal logistic regression estimates the association between profile membership and the preference for market justice in education, net of sociodemographic and political controls.

### Latent profile analysis

LPA is a person-centered finite mixture model. It assumes that a population that looks homogeneous is in fact a mixture of a small number of unobserved subgroups, and it uses the pattern of responses to a set of indicators to estimate each respondent's probability of belonging to each subgroup [@jason_handbook_2015]. This fits the aim of the study, which is not to place respondents on a single meritocracy scale but to uncover qualitatively different combinations of perceptions and preferences, such as endorsing meritocracy while also perceiving or accepting privilege. LPA and latent class analysis (LCA) are very similar and share the same fit statistics. They differ in the type of indicator: LCA is designed for categorical indicators and describes classes by conditional probabilities of endorsement, whereas LPA is used for continuous indicators and describes profiles by their mean on each indicator [@jason_handbook_2015; @scottorosato_latent_2012]. The eight items are four-point Likert responses. LPA is used because they are treated as continuous, which retains the intensity of agreement that dichotomizing the items for an LCA would discard. Treating ordinal items with four categories as continuous is a common simplification, but it is an assumption and a limitation of this specification.

Solutions with one to five profiles are estimated in R with the `tidyLPA` package, using maximum likelihood estimated through the Expectation-Maximization algorithm and random starting values, with a fixed seed for reproducibility. The number of profiles is chosen by combining statistical and substantive criteria, since no single index is decisive:

1. **Information criteria.** AIC and BIC are compared across solutions, with lower values indicating better fit. BIC has been identified as the most reliable index for selecting the number of classes. Because these indices tend to keep decreasing as profiles are added, the size of each improvement relative to the K−1 solution is examined, and a marginal gain suggests that an extra profile adds little.
2. **Classification quality.** Relative entropy (0 to 1) assesses how clearly respondents are separated into profiles, with higher values indicating more accurate classification. After selecting the solution, the mean posterior probability of the assigned profile is reported for each profile.
3. **Profile size.** The proportion of the smallest profile is examined, and solutions with very small profiles are viewed with caution because they tend to be unstable.
4. **Interpretability.** The final decision depends on whether the profiles make theoretical sense and differ qualitatively, not only quantitatively, in their pattern of means.

A class or profile is a statistical construct, not necessarily a real group. Spurious profiles can arise from non-normality or from misspecification of the model, so the profiles are interpreted as useful descriptions of belief configurations and not as proof of tangible subgroups.

### Ordinal logistic regression

After selecting the number of profiles, each respondent is assigned to the profile with the highest posterior probability (modal assignment). Preference for market justice in education, a five-category ordered response, is then regressed on profile membership with ordinal (proportional-odds) logistic regression, estimated with the MASS package in R. Results are reported as odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals, and the reference category is the *Partial meritocrats* profile.

Seven models are estimated. Model 1 includes only profile membership. Model 2 adds sex, university education and income quintile, and Model 3 adds political identification. Models 4 to 6 add to Model 3 the interaction of profile with each political category (left, center and right, respectively, with those who do not identify with any position as reference), and Model 7 adds the interaction of profile with university education. The interactions examine whether the association between profile and the outcome varies across these groups. Each political interaction is estimated in a separate model so that their effects do not overlap.

Modal assignment treats profile membership as known, although it is estimated with error, which tends to attenuate the association with the outcome. The mean posterior probability of each profile is reported as an indicator of how large this uncertainty is.

### Robustness analysis

to prevent latent profiles from being an artifice due to suspicious response patterns, Respondents flagged as careless responders were excluded before estimation. Three indices were computed on the eight items (longstring, intra-individual response variability and Mahalanobis distance), and respondents flagged by at least two of them were removed, as were those with missing values on any indicator [@ward_dealing_2023; @curran_methods_2016]. The resulting sample is far above the minimum of about 100 cases usually recommended for mixture models.
